what_its_for: Burosumab-Twza is used to treat a rare condition called X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH), which causes low phosphate levels in your blood. Low phosphate can make your bones weak, cause pain, and affect how you walk. This medicine helps your kidneys hold onto phosphate so your body can use it to build stronger bones. It may also be used for a condition called tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) in adults when the tumor cannot be removed.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under your skin (subcutaneous injection). A healthcare provider, doctor, or nurse will give you the injection, usually in your upper arm, thigh, belly area, or buttocks. The injection site will be rotated each time to avoid skin irritation. Do not inject into skin that is red, bruised, tender, or scarred.
dosing: For children with XLH, the dose is based on your child's body weight and is given every 2 weeks. For adults with XLH or TIO, the dose is also based on body weight and is typically given every 4 weeks. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you and may adjust it based on your phosphate blood levels. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss an appointment to get your injection, call your doctor or healthcare provider as soon as possible to reschedule. Try not to skip doses, because keeping phosphate levels steady is important for your treatment to work well. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Burosumab-Twza is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or clinic. If you are given vials to take home, store them in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep the vials in the original carton to protect them from light. Do not shake the vials. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not take phosphate supplements or active forms of vitamin D (such as calcitriol or alfacalcidol) while using this medicine unless your doctor specifically tells you to. Taking these together can raise your phosphate and calcium levels too high, which can be harmful to your kidneys. Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you are taking before starting burosumab-Twza.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: serious allergic reaction signs such as rash, itching, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, dizziness, or trouble breathing; signs of high phosphate or calcium such as muscle cramps, tingling or numbness, nausea, vomiting, or confusion; pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site that does not go away; bone or joint pain that gets significantly worse; or any new or unusual symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Burosumab-Twza starts working to raise your phosphate levels fairly quickly, sometimes within weeks of starting treatment. However, improvements in bone strength, pain, and physical function may take several months to notice. Children may see improvements in bone growth and the way they walk over time. It is important to keep all your appointments and blood tests so your doctor can monitor how well the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Children: This medicine can be used in children 6 months of age and older with XLH. Doses are carefully calculated based on the child's weight and adjusted as the child grows. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine is safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Kidney problems: This medicine is not recommended for people with severe kidney disease or those on dialysis. Older adults: There is limited information about use in older adults, so your doctor will monitor you closely.
